q: The 3-mediator gadget converges empirically as Delta^{-0.41}, steeper than the paper's worst-case Delta^{-1/3} bound. Is this super-linear improvement a generic feature of 'benign' random Y instances with reasonable spectral density, or is our seed-0 Y atypical?
basis: Fitted log-log slope = -0.41 in Delta (equivalently +1.24 in delta) over 200 <= Delta <= 1e5 on a single seed-0 pseudo-random 2-local Y; the paper's Eq. 14 remainder is only O(delta) worst case.
next_steps: Repeat the Delta-sweep for 1000 random seeds of Y (fixed 3-local B1 B2 B3), tabulate slope distribution; also test structured Y (transverse-field Ising, Heisenberg) to see whether spectrum shape controls the effective exponent.

q: Our ground-state error saturates near 5e-2 at Delta >= 1e5. How much of this floor is the finite O(delta)-coefficient constant versus numpy.linalg.eigh's small-eigenvalue relative-error conditioning against a Delta-scale penalty spectrum?
basis: Error decreases monotonically from 5.5 (Delta=5) to 3.3e-2 (Delta=5e5) but the last decade only halves the error; log-log slope drops from -0.6 to -0.2 in the last decade, suggesting a floor.
next_steps: Repeat with mpmath (100-digit) eigendecomposition, and separately with an explicit Schur complement onto the C = span{|000>_m,|111>_m} subspace (dim 2^n_data*2 = 16 instead of 64) which analytically removes the Delta-scale eigenvalues; if the mpmath curve keeps dropping past Delta=1e5 while numpy's flattens, the floor is numerical.

q: The KKR gadget uses three mediator qubits per 3-local target term. Bravyi (2008) and Cao-Nagaj (2015) proposed more compact 'shrinking' constructions. How does the empirical Delta-scaling of ground-state error compare across these gadgets at fixed physical qubit count?
basis: Our reproduction uses 3 mediators per gadget and shows an O(delta) error; the paper explicitly notes (Sec. 6.3) that sequential application would blow norms exponentially, motivating norm-efficient alternatives.
next_steps: Implement the Bravyi-Nagaj 1-mediator variant and the Cao-Nagaj perturbative gadget on the same seed-0 Y - 6 B1 B2 B3 target, sweep Delta on 6-qubit total systems, compare ground-state error curves and the effective constant in front of the O(delta) bound.

q: KKR's Theorem 3 requires ||V|| << Delta. Our numerics show a spectacular failure at Delta = 5, 10 (error ~ 5) that shrinks to O(delta) at Delta >= 200. What is the empirical functional form of the ground-state error across the ||V|| ~ Delta crossover, and is it well-approximated by a universal rational-function or Pade-like curve?
basis: At Delta=5, err = 5.5 ~ full spectral spread of H_target; at Delta=200, err = 0.81; at Delta=1000, err = 0.11 -- suggesting a sharp but smooth crossover near Delta ~ ||V|| ~ 10-50 for this instance.
next_steps: Sample err(Delta) on a much denser log grid (say 100 points per decade over Delta in [1, 1e4]) and fit to candidate forms err = a*delta / (1 + b*delta^p) etc.; test whether coefficients (a,b,p) are instance-independent when scaled by ||V||.

q: Section 6.3 argues that sequential (rather than simultaneous) 3-to-2-local reduction gives an exponential norm blowup because each gadget rescales operator norms. Can this be verified numerically by applying the gadget construction sequentially to a small multi-3-local-term Hamiltonian, e.g. 5 3-local terms on 6 qubits, and measuring norm growth vs simultaneous application?
basis: Our replication only exercises a single 3-local term (Y - 6 B1 B2 B3). The paper's Section 6.3 sequential-vs-simultaneous distinction is untested here, and it is the argument that makes the whole reduction polynomial rather than exponential.
next_steps: Build a small target H_target = Y + sum_{k=1..5} c_k B_{k,1} B_{k,2} B_{k,3} on 6 data qubits; apply the KKR gadget once to all 5 terms in parallel (needs 15 mediators, 21 qubits total = 2^21 dim; borderline feasible) vs sequentially (5 applications of 3 mediators each, one at a time), measure ||V||, ||H_eff|| growth, and required Delta for a fixed target error.
